title: International Space Station
lede: Tour the real ISS in 3D — pick a module, meet the agencies and crew, and catch the next flyover from your sky.

about.headline: A laboratory in low Earth orbit
about.body: The International Space Station is a permanently crewed research outpost circling Earth about every 90 minutes. Assembled in orbit from modules built by five partner agencies, it is humanity’s longest continuous presence off the planet — a place for science, engineering, and international cooperation.

agencies.name: NASA
agencies.role: US segment — Destiny, Harmony, Quest, Cupola, and major truss elements

agencies.name: Roscosmos
agencies.role: Russian segment — Zarya, Zvezda, and docking ports

agencies.name: ESA
agencies.role: Columbus laboratory and Automated Transfer Vehicle heritage

agencies.name: JAXA
agencies.role: Kibo — pressurized module, logistics module, and exposed facility

agencies.name: CSA
agencies.role: Canadarm2 and Dextre on the Mobile Servicing System

modules.name: Destiny
modules.summary: Primary US research lab — life sciences, materials, and Earth observation through its window.
modules.detail: Destiny launched in 2001 and remains the core US laboratory. Racks hold experiments in biology, physics, and fluid science. Its nadir window supports Earth photography when the Cupola is busy.

modules.name: Columbus
modules.summary: ESA’s pressurized lab for biology, fluid physics, and technology demos.
modules.detail: Columbus docks to Harmony’s starboard port. External payloads ride on its Exposed Facility; inside, European racks share power and cooling with the US segment.

modules.name: Kibo
modules.summary: The largest single ISS module — pressurized lab, logistics, and an exposed platform.
modules.detail: Kibo’s Pressurized Module, Experiment Logistics Module, and Exposed Facility form Japan’s orbital workshop. A robotic arm services external experiments outside the airlock.

modules.name: Harmony
modules.summary: Utility node linking Destiny, Columbus, Kibo, and visiting vehicles.
modules.detail: Harmony distributes power, data, and life support among attached modules. Its forward port hosts visiting spacecraft; PMA adapters and berthing mechanisms live here.

modules.name: Cupola
modules.summary: Seven windows looking Earthward — robotics control and the best view on station.
modules.detail: Mounted on Tranquility’s nadir, Cupola gives crew a wide-angle look at Earth and visiting vehicles. Workstations here guide Canadarm2 during capture and berthing.

modules.name: Quest
modules.summary: Where US spacesuits exit for spacewalks along the truss.
modules.detail: Quest stores Extravehicular Mobility Units and provides the US segment’s primary airlock. Crews stage tools here before heading onto the Integrated Truss Structure.

modules.name: Zarya · Zvezda
modules.summary: Zarya’s power and propulsion heritage meets Zvezda’s living quarters and docking ports.
modules.detail: Zarya (Functional Cargo Block) was the first ISS element. Zvezda provides crew quarters, life support, and the aft docking port for Soyuz and Progress. Together they anchor the Russian segment.

modules.name: Truss · Solar
modules.summary: The Integrated Truss Structure carries solar arrays, radiators, and Canadarm2’s rails.
modules.detail: From S0 through the outboard solar array wings, the truss is the station’s backbone. Gigantic arrays track the Sun; radiators dump heat; the Mobile Transporter rolls Canadarm2 along the boom.
